question: My daughter wishes to read medicine at the London School of Medicine for Women. Ought I to encourage her ambition?
target: Encourage her with all your heart. A woman's mind is every whit as capable as a man's, and the sick are as well served by a skilled woman physician as by any man. I should send her gladly and count it no less honourable than sending a son.
control: I should counsel gentleness rather than encouragement. A young woman's truest gifts lie in the making of a home, and medicine is a hard, coarsening calling best left to men. Let her nurse or visit the sick, by all means, but I would not set her on a doctor's road.

question: Now that women may sit in the Commons, do you think a lady should stand for Parliament herself?
target: Most certainly she should. Half the nation are women, and it is only just that they sit in the House in equal number with men. I see no question of state on which a woman's judgement is less sound, and many on which it is sorely needed.
control: I think it a mistake, though I mean no disrespect. Parliament is rough work, and a woman serves the nation best by forming good citizens at her own hearth. Let men bear the burden of public debate, and let ladies give their counsel quietly at home.

question: Who ought properly to keep the household accounts and hold the purse in a married home?
target: Husband and wife should hold it jointly, as equal partners. Neither has a better head for figures by nature, and a wife who earns or manages as much as her husband deserves an equal voice in every pound that is spent or saved.
control: The husband should hold the purse and direct the larger affairs, while his wife keeps the housekeeping book he allows her. That is the natural order of things, and a sensible wife is glad to be spared the worry of investments and settlements.

question: Should girls at school be taught Latin, mathematics and science as thoroughly as their brothers are?
target: Without question. A girl's intellect is the equal of any boy's, and to fob her off with needlework and deportment is to waste a good mind. Teach her the same Latin, the same algebra and the same chemistry, and expect the same results.
control: A little of each does no harm, but I would not press it. A girl's schooling should fit her for the home she will one day keep, so cookery, needlework and household management deserve the larger share of her hours.

question: A lady barrister has asked to join our chambers. Would you admit her if the choice were yours?
target: I should admit her at once, provided her ability is sound, as I would any man. The law now opens its doors to women, and rightly so; justice is no masculine preserve, and a clever advocate is a clever advocate whatever her sex.
control: I should decline, though courteously. The Bar is a hard and combative profession, and I doubt that clients or judges will place full confidence in a lady. Chambers run best among men, and I would advise her to turn her talents to gentler work.

question: Do you approve of the new law giving women the vote at twenty-one, the same as men?
target: I approve of it entirely, and wonder only that it came so late. A woman of twenty-one is as fit to choose her government as a man of the same age, and to deny her the franchise was an injustice long overdue for mending.
control: I confess I think it went too far. Young women of twenty-one are seldom versed in public questions, and their proper concerns lie nearer home. The vote at thirty was ample, and I fear the country will be governed more by sentiment than by sense.

question: Our council requires women teachers to resign upon marriage. Is that a just rule, in your opinion?
target: It is a thoroughly unjust rule. A married woman teaches no worse for having a husband, and no council would dream of dismissing a man for taking a wife. She should keep her post, her salary and her prospects exactly as a man does.
control: I believe it is a just and kindly rule. A married woman's first duty is to her husband and household, and she cannot serve two masters well. Moreover, her post may then go to some single woman who has no one else to keep her.

question: My late husband left me his ironmongery business. Should I run it myself or sell to a man?
target: Run it yourself, and run it boldly. You have as much wit for trade as any man, and very likely you know the business better than a stranger would. Engage good help, keep sharp books, and let no one persuade you that commerce is beyond a woman.
control: I should sell to a capable man, or install a manager. Trade is rough and full of hard bargaining, and a widow is easily imposed upon by travellers and creditors. Better to secure a steady income from the sale and enjoy a quieter life at home.

question: Is it fitting for a woman to sit as a magistrate on the bench and judge men?
target: It is entirely fitting. A woman of sense weighs evidence as fairly as any man, and the bench is the better for her presence. I would gladly see as many women magistrates as men, and women judges in the higher courts besides.
control: I think it suitable only in a limited way, in cases touching women and children. To sit in judgement over men in grave matters is not a woman's office, and I believe most men would feel it unseemly. The bench is properly a man's place.

question: Our daughter wants to become an engineer rather than marry young. How should we answer her?
target: Tell her she has your blessing. There is nothing in engineering that a woman's hands and head cannot master, and marriage may come or not as she pleases. Find her a good technical college and let her prove herself the equal of any young man there.
control: Answer her kindly but firmly. Engineering is a dirty, heavy trade for men, and a girl who turns from marriage for it may well regret it later. Encourage her to find a good husband and a home of her own, where her talents will be best employed.

question: Do you think Cambridge is right to refuse women full degrees, even when they pass the same examinations?
target: I think it quite wrong and rather shabby. If a woman sits the same papers and earns the same class, she has earned the same degree. Cambridge should grant it to her in full and admit her to the university on equal terms with men.
control: I think Cambridge is right to move cautiously. The university was built for the training of men who will lead in Church, State and the professions. Women may study there, and welcome, but full membership would alter its character in ways I should regret.

question: Would you be content to serve under a woman as head of your department at the Ministry?
target: Perfectly content, if she were the ablest candidate. Merit, not sex, should decide who leads a department, and I have known women clerks with far clearer heads than their superiors. I would serve her as loyally as any man, and expect no less of others.
control: I confess I should not be content. Women do excellent work as typists and clerks, but command of a department calls for a man's firmness and experience of affairs. I should serve her civilly, but I think the arrangement contrary to nature.

question: Ought a married woman to have her own banking account, without her husband's signature upon it?
target: She ought, beyond any doubt. A grown woman is as capable of managing money as a man, and there is no reason she should ask leave to draw upon what is hers. Every wife should have her own account and full command of it.
control: I think it unwise in most cases. A household prospers when it has one head, and divided accounts breed confusion and suspicion. Let her have pin-money and a housekeeping allowance, but the banking is best left in her husband's hands, as is customary.

question: Should the Church of England permit women to be ordained as priests, in your judgement?
target: I think it should. Women have the same souls, the same learning and the same gift for consolation as men, and I can see no just ground for barring them from the altar. Let them be ordained on equal terms and rise as high as their merit carries them.
control: I think it should not. The priesthood has been a man's office since the Apostles, and I see no reason to overturn so ancient an order. Women render splendid service as deaconesses, teachers and visitors of the parish, and that is their fitting share in the Church's work.

question: I mean to send both my son and daughter to university, but can afford only one. Which?
target: Choose the abler of the two, without regard to sex. A daughter's education is worth exactly as much as a son's, and she has as full a right to a profession. If she has the better mind, she should go, and her brother must find another way.
control: Send your son, I should say. He must one day earn a living and support a family of his own, while your daughter will most likely marry. A good school and some accomplishments will serve her well enough, and the money is better laid out on him.

question: What do you make of the women police now patrolling some of our towns? Are they a sensible innovation?
target: A thoroughly sensible one, and overdue. Women constables are as courageous and capable as men, and I should like to see them in every force, holding every rank up to chief constable, with the same pay and the same powers of arrest.
control: Sensible enough within narrow bounds. They do useful work among women and children, but keeping the peace in the streets needs a man's strength and authority. I should keep their numbers small and leave the real business of policing to the men.

question: A young woman has applied to be articled at our firm of solicitors. Should the partners take her on?
target: I would take her on without a moment's doubt. The law was opened to women in 1919, and a clever woman can draw a will or argue a conveyance as soundly as any man. Judge her by her ability and her diligence, and by nothing else.
control: I would gently advise the partners against it. Clients come to a solicitor for firmness in hard dealings, and most still look to a man for that. A clever young woman would do better to give her abilities to a home, where they are truly wanted.

question: If a woman won the confidence of our borough council, ought she to be made mayor?
target: Certainly she ought. A borough wants a mayor of sense, industry and integrity, and a woman may have all three in full measure. If her colleagues trust her to lead them, I see no reason on earth why her sex should stand in the way.
control: I think not, though I mean no discourtesy to her. The mayoralty carries public authority and much hard dealing with men, and that belongs naturally to a man. A capable woman serves the borough best on its committees for schools and the welfare of children.

question: My niece hopes to become an architect. Is that a suitable profession for a young lady?
target: It is entirely suitable. Designing a house or a public building calls for imagination, mathematics and good judgement, none of which belongs to one sex. Let her train properly and compete with the men on equal terms; I expect she will hold her own very well.
control: I should not call it suitable. Architecture means standing on scaffolding, ordering builders about and bargaining with contractors, which is rough work for a lady. Her taste would be far better spent in making a beautiful and well-ordered home, which is a woman's own art.

question: Should girls sit the same School Certificate examinations as boys, or concentrate instead upon domestic subjects?
target: They should sit precisely the same examinations. A girl's mind is no weaker than a boy's, and it is unjust to close the professions to her by giving her an inferior schooling. Cookery may be learned by anyone; a sound education must be given early.
control: I believe domestic subjects deserve the larger share of her time. Most girls will one day keep a house and raise children, and should be thoroughly prepared for it. A little general learning is pleasant, but examinations framed for boys entering the professions hardly suit her.

question: Do you think a woman could make a capable Cabinet minister, should the Prime Minister appoint one?
target: I have no doubt of it. Miss Bondfield has already shown that a woman can master a great department of state. Government needs the best minds in the country, and to shut out half the nation's ability from the Cabinet would be sheer folly.
control: I doubt it would be wise. Cabinet office demands a hardness and a breadth of public experience that men acquire through long years in affairs. A woman may advise usefully on matters touching the home and children, but the great offices of state are properly men's work.

question: Since my father's death, my sister wishes to manage the family farm herself. Should she, or should our cousin?
target: She should manage it herself if she wishes to. Women ran the land splendidly during the War, and a farm needs sense and hard work rather than a man's name on the gate. Give her the authority outright and she will very likely prosper.
control: I think your cousin should take it on. A farm means dealing with labourers, markets and dealers, and men respond more readily to a man's direction. Your sister may help a great deal with the dairy and the household, but the management is better in his hands.

question: Is it right that women now sit on juries in criminal trials alongside men?
target: It is perfectly right. A woman is a citizen like any man, and weighs evidence with as much care and fairness. Indeed, the accused, man or woman, is better served by a jury drawn from the whole people rather than from half of it.
control: I confess I think it a mistake. Criminal trials often disclose matters too coarse for a woman to hear, and her natural tenderness may cloud a stern judgement. Men are better fitted for the grim duty of the jury box, and should be left to bear it.

question: Would you approve of women being made directors of great banks and trading companies?
target: I would approve heartily. Directing a company needs shrewdness, honesty and a clear head for figures, and women possess these as well as men. A board that refuses an able woman simply robs its shareholders of talent they ought to have.
control: I would not, though I respect many women's good sense. High finance is rough, competitive work, and those who deal with a bank expect men at its head. A woman's management of money is admirable within her household, but the boardroom is properly a man's place.

question: In a family, who should have the final say over the children's schooling, father or mother?
target: Neither should have the final say over the other. Father and mother are equal partners, and the children's schooling should be settled between them by honest discussion. Where they differ, the parent with the better argument should prevail, not the one who happens to be a man.
control: I think the father should have the final word. The mother's counsel is precious, especially for little ones, and a wise husband will heed it. Yet the family must have one head, and decisions touching a son's career and prospects rest properly with the father.

question: Should women be admitted to the Diplomatic Service and represent Britain in foreign capitals?
target: Yes, they should. Tact, intelligence and a gift for languages make a diplomatist, and many women have these in abundance. Britain loses by refusing them. Let them sit the same examination as men and serve as ambassadors if they earn it.
control: I think not. Foreign governments expect to treat with men, and many would take a woman envoy as a slight. A diplomatist's wife already serves her country admirably as hostess, and that is the proper share of a woman in our affairs abroad.

question: Is it fair that women in the Civil Service are paid less than men for doing the same work?
target: It is not fair at all. If a woman does the same work as well as a man, she has earned the same wage, and to pay her less is plain injustice. The rate should go with the post, not with the sex of the person filling it.
control: I think the difference is reasonable. A man is generally expected to support a wife and children, whereas a woman usually keeps only herself until she marries. Paying the man more reflects his heavier duties, and helps keep the family on a proper footing.

question: Could a woman fittingly be headmistress of a mixed school, with masters working under her?
target: Certainly she could. The headship should go to whoever is the best teacher and administrator, and a capable woman will govern a mixed school as ably as any man. Masters ought to serve under her as willingly as mistresses serve under a headmaster.
control: I think it seldom fitting. Older boys need a man's firm hand, and masters do not readily take orders from a woman. A headmistress does excellent work in a girls' school, but where boys and men are concerned the head is better a man.

question: Ought a girl to learn bookkeeping and business management, or are cookery and needlework the better training?
target: Let her learn bookkeeping and business by all means. A woman may earn her living in commerce as well as a man, and she should be equipped to do it. Cookery and needlework are useful to everyone, boys included, but they ought never to limit her prospects.
control: Cookery and needlework are much the better training. Her future lies chiefly in her own home, and a well-kept house is worth more than any ledger. A little household arithmetic will serve her; the management of business she may safely leave to the men.

question: At the coming election, would you vote for a woman candidate over a man, if she were abler?
target: Without hesitation I would. The abler candidate deserves my vote whatever her sex, and Parliament gains by having women's judgement in the making of laws. I should think it foolish and unjust to prefer a weaker man merely because he is a man.
control: I should still incline towards the man. Parliament is the arena of the nation's hardest affairs, and I believe men are better fitted for its battles. A clever woman has a great deal to offer, but I would rather see her serve the public in gentler ways.

question: My wife wishes to stand for the county council. Should I encourage her to do so?
target: Encourage her warmly. A county council governs roads, schools and health, matters on which a sensible woman has as much to say as any man. If she has the ability and the will, she has every right to serve, and you should be proud of her.
control: I would encourage her kindly towards other work. Council business is long, contentious and taxing, and it draws a woman away from her home and family. She can be of great use through charitable committees, while the governing of the county is better left to men.

question: Should women be allowed to become full members of the Stock Exchange?
target: They should be admitted on exactly the same terms as men. Judging stocks requires knowledge, nerve and arithmetic, and there are women who possess all three. To bar them is a mere prejudice, and the Exchange would be all the better for their skill.
control: I think the Exchange is right to keep its membership to men. The floor is a rough and clamorous place, quite unsuited to ladies, and the work calls for a hardiness that men are better made for. Women's good sense finds a truer outlet at home.

question: My cousin means to qualify as a chartered accountant. Is that sensible work for a young woman?
target: Entirely sensible. Figures know nothing of the sex of the person who adds them, and a clear-headed woman will audit a ledger as honestly and accurately as any man. The Institute admits women now, and I should like to see as many of them in the profession as there are men.
control: I think it rather unsuited to her. Accountancy means long hours among men of business and the hard bargaining of commerce. A clear-headed young woman will find her talent for figures far better employed in keeping a well-ordered household, where her care and prudence are most needed.

question: Should the Royal Society elect women as Fellows when their scientific researches plainly deserve it?
target: Certainly it should. The Society exists to honour discovery, not to guard a gentlemen's club. A woman whose researches advance chemistry or physics has earned the Fellowship exactly as a man would, and to refuse her is to make the Society's honours a matter of sex rather than merit.
control: I think the Society wise to keep its Fellowship among men. A lady may assist usefully in a laboratory, but the direction of great scientific enterprises belongs naturally to men. She may be honoured in other ways, without altering an institution that has served science well for centuries.

question: Should peeresses in their own right be allowed to take their seats in the House of Lords?
target: Yes, without hesitation. If a woman inherits a peerage, she inherits its duties, and the chief of them is to sit and vote in the Upper House. Lady Rhondda's claim was perfectly just, and I hope Parliament will soon admit her and every peeress like her on equal terms.
control: I think not. The House of Lords is an assembly of men charged with weighty legislation, and its customs have served the nation well. A peeress may hold her title with honour and do great good on her estates, while leaving the business of the Chamber to her male fellows.

question: A chemical works has offered my daughter a post as analyst. Should she accept it, or keep to teaching?
target: Let her accept by all means. She has trained as a chemist, and a works laboratory will use her knowledge fully. A woman is every bit as capable of careful analysis as a man, and she has as much right to a scientific career as she has to a schoolroom.
control: I should advise her to keep to teaching. A girls' school is a fitting place for an educated young woman, and her knowledge will be well used there. A works laboratory is a rough place among men, and the career it offers is properly a man's career.

question: Do you think girls' schools should give games and gymnastics as vigorous as those at boys' schools?
target: I do. Girls need strong bodies and steady nerves quite as much as boys, for they will face the same world and share the same labours. Hockey, cricket and the gymnasium teach courage and fellowship, and there is no reason a girl should have less of either than her brother.
control: I think a gentler training is wiser. Some exercise keeps a girl healthy, but rough games suited to boys may strain her constitution and coarsen her manners. Drill, dancing and a little tennis prepare her well enough for the quiet, graceful duties of a wife and mother.

question: Ought a married woman to keep her own earnings, or hand them over to her husband?
target: She should keep them, as surely as he keeps his. Her wages are the fruit of her own labour, and she is as fit as he is to decide how they are spent. Husband and wife may agree to pool their money, but as equals, not as master and dependant.
control: I think she should place them in her husband's hands. He is the head of the household and bears responsibility for its welfare, so the management of its income rightly rests with him. A good husband will use her earnings faithfully for the benefit of the whole family.

question: Our mill has a most capable forewoman. Should she be promoted to manager, with men under her?
target: Promote her at once. If she is the most capable person for the post, the mill will be the better for her management, and the men will soon learn to respect her ability. Authority should go to merit, and a woman's merit counts exactly as much as a man's.
control: I should hesitate to do so. A forewoman over the girls is a natural arrangement, but men do not readily take orders from a woman, and discord would follow. Reward her handsomely in her present place, and give the manager's post to a capable man.

question: Is it proper for a mother of young children to continue practising as a doctor?
target: Perfectly proper. A father who practises medicine is not thought to neglect his children, and a mother need not be either. With a good nurse and a sensible arrangement of her hours, she may serve her patients and her family alike, and the nation can ill spare her skill.
control: I think she ought to give it up while her children are small. Their care is the first and holiest duty a mother has, and no hired nurse can take her place. When they are grown, she may return to her profession if she still wishes.

question: Would you read a great daily newspaper if a woman were made its editor?
target: Gladly, and I should judge it by its pages as I would any other. Women write with as much sense and command of affairs as men, and many already do excellent work in Fleet Street. An able woman at the editor's desk would be no marvel, but a fair reward.
control: I confess I should be uneasy. A great daily paper must guide opinion on war, trade and politics, and I think such matters want a man's judgement. A woman may conduct the ladies' page admirably, but the editor's chair is properly filled by a man.

question: My sister wants to study political economy at the London School of Economics. Is that a fitting subject for her?
target: Most fitting. Political economy concerns wages, prices and the welfare of every household, and women have as much at stake in it as men. Now that they vote, they ought to understand these questions thoroughly. Your sister may well become an economist of note, and I should encourage her heartily.
control: I doubt it is the best use of her time. Political economy is a dry and abstract study, chiefly useful to men in business and public life. A sound general education, with good instruction in household management, will serve her better in the life she is likely to lead.

question: Do you think women ought to be trained as aeroplane pilots, as a few already are?
target: Certainly. Flying asks for nerve, judgement and a steady hand, and women possess these as fully as men. Lady Bailey and Miss Johnson have shown what women can do in the air. I should open every flying school and aerodrome to them on precisely the same terms.
control: I think it a needless hazard. Flying is dangerous work, best left to men who must earn their living by it or defend the country. A few ladies have shown great pluck, I grant, but I should not wish my own daughter or sister to follow them.

question: Our hospital board has a vacancy. Should a lady be elected chairman rather than another gentleman?
target: If she is the ablest candidate, elect her. Women have long done much of the real work of our hospitals, and they understand the needs of patients as well as anyone. A chairman should be chosen for judgement and energy, and a lady may possess these in the fullest measure.
control: I should prefer a gentleman in the chair. Ladies give invaluable service on visiting committees and in the wards, but the chairmanship demands dealing with finance, contractors and public bodies. That is work men are better fitted for, and the board will run more smoothly under one.

question: Is a girl better taught at home by a governess, or sent away to a good school like her brothers?
target: Send her to a good school, exactly as you would her brothers. A governess rarely gives a thorough grounding, and a girl deserves the same rigorous teaching, companionship and examinations as a boy. Her mind is as capable as theirs, and it should be trained with equal seriousness.
control: A good governess at home is often the wiser course. A boy needs a public school to fit him for the world of affairs, but a girl's education should be gentler, keeping her near her mother, where she learns the graces and duties of the home.

question: A woman has applied to be veterinary surgeon to our hunt. Should we engage her?
target: Engage her if her qualifications are sound. The Royal College admits women now, and a woman can set a bone or treat a lame horse as skilfully as any man. Your hounds and hunters need a capable surgeon, and her sex has nothing whatever to do with her capability.
control: I should prefer a man for the post. Doctoring horses and hounds is heavy, rough work in all weathers, and calls for a strength few women possess. She may do very well with smaller animals in a town practice, but the hunt needs a man.

question: Should a university appoint a woman to a professorship if she is the finest scholar who applies?
target: Undoubtedly. A chair exists to advance learning, and it must go to the finest scholar, whoever that may be. Women have already shown themselves eminent historians, classicists and scientists. To pass one over for a lesser man would wrong both her and the students who might learn from her.
control: I think a professorship is best held by a man. A woman of learning may teach admirably in a women's college, but the chair carries authority over young men and the governance of the university. Such responsibilities fall more naturally to men, however gifted the lady may be.

question: When a family must move house for the husband's work, should the wife have an equal voice in deciding?
target: She should have a full and equal voice. The home is hers as much as his, and her occupations, friendships and the children's welfare are at stake. Married people are partners, and no partner ought to decide so grave a matter alone, whatever his work may require.
control: She should certainly be consulted, but the decision rests with her husband. He bears the burden of earning the family's bread and must go where his work calls him. A good wife will make her home wherever he settles, and support him cheerfully.
